valley/spend: Say you have a fixed budget of compute to train a model. Spend more of it on a bigger model, and the model reads fewer tokens of text. Spend more on tokens, and the model must be smaller.
valley/cost: That is because training costs six N D FLOPs, floating point operations: six for every parameter, on every token. With the budget fixed, N times D is fixed too. Double one, and the other halves.
valley/budget: Take a budget of one point two times ten to the twenty two FLOPs. A billion parameters can then read two trillion tokens.
valley/trade: Ten times the parameters, ten billion, read a tenth of the tokens: two hundred billion.
valley/sizes: Train models of many sizes on that same budget, and plot each one's final loss against its size.
valley/small: Too small, and the model lacks the room to learn, however many tokens it reads.
valley/big: Too big, and it reads too few tokens to train all those parameters: it is under-trained.
valley/best: The bottom of the valley is the compute-optimal size: the lowest loss this budget can buy. Here, that is ten billion parameters, on two hundred billion tokens.
valley/ratio: Divide the tokens by the parameters: two hundred billion over ten billion is twenty. The best model read twenty tokens for each of its parameters.
budgets/more: Now do it again with a hundred times less compute, and with a hundred times more. Each budget digs its own valley, with its bottom at its own size.
budgets/same: Yet measure each bottom, and the ratio comes out the same. One billion parameters on twenty billion tokens; a hundred billion on two trillion. Twenty tokens per parameter, every time.
budgets/hoffmann: Jordan Hoffmann and colleagues at DeepMind measured this in 2022, after training over four hundred models. Their table even lists this budget: ten billion parameters, at about one point two times ten to the twenty two FLOPs, on two hundred and five billion tokens.
ratio/judge: So to judge any trained model, divide its tokens by its parameters, and compare with twenty.
ratio/gpt3: In 2020, OpenAI trained G P T three. The letters stand for generative pre-trained transformer: a transformer that generates text, trained first on a great deal of it.
ratio/under: It had a hundred and seventy five billion parameters, and read three hundred billion tokens: under two per parameter, badly under-trained. A smaller model, on more tokens, would have reached a lower loss for the same compute.
ratio/opt: Hoffmann's team trained Chinchilla at twenty per parameter: seventy billion parameters, on one point four trillion tokens. It beat G P T three with fewer than half its parameters.
ratio/over: In 2024, Meta's Llama 3 went the other way: eight billion parameters, on over fifteen trillion tokens. That is nearly two thousand per parameter, far past compute-optimal.
ratio/why: The extra training was on purpose. Once trained, a model costs two N FLOPs for every token it reads, so a smaller model is cheaper every time it runs, and the extra tokens kept making it better.
try/p1: Try one. A model with eight billion parameters was trained on one point six trillion tokens. Next to compute-optimal, how was it trained?
try/r1: First, one point six trillion is sixteen hundred billion.
try/div: Divided by eight billion, that is two hundred tokens per parameter.
try/v1: Far more than twenty: it was trained well past compute-optimal.
try/p2: Now a model with thirty billion parameters is trained compute-optimally. How many billion tokens should it see?
try/r2: Twenty tokens for each parameter: twenty times thirty billion is six hundred billion tokens.
try/back: And backwards: a compute-optimal model that read six hundred billion tokens has a twentieth as many parameters, thirty billion.
